### Three More Dead in Kraków, a Judge Jails Peña, and Tankers Burn in Hormuz

Filed as: Edition No. 18 — The Midnight Watch · 2026-11-08T00:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-08-midnight-watch.html

The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Three More Dead in Kraków, a Judge Jails Peña, and Tankers Burn in Hormuz

 The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: Saturday settled the detention question in Asunción, where a judge ordered the removed president and the former central bank chief held before trial, and it settled Berkshire Hathaway’s quarter on paper. It deepened the Kraków case, where police searching the suspect’s home found three more bodies, and it closed with explosions across Iran’s Hormuz coast, two tankers reported on fire, and an American disabling of a vessel in the Gulf of Oman—while the larger Iran decision, the Senate count, and the Abu Dhabi talks all stayed open, waiting on Tuesday.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 16, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Saturday, and in the day’s earlier editions, Nos. 14 and 15. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Saturday Settled, What It Left Open

Saturday settled a detention, a quarter’s accounts, and nothing else it was asked to settle. In Asunción, Judge Humberto Otazú ordered former President Santiago Peña held in pretrial detention at a military facility and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo held in a detention center, a ruling the Evening Watch left pending at 1800; Mr. Peña’s attorney said he is pleading not guilty. In Kraków, the day’s count of the dead grew by three without a shot in the square: police searching the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski found two women and a man dead, and the prime minister told a late briefing there are strong indications the three are members of the suspect’s immediate family. The six dead in the Main Market Square stand as filed at evening—four women and two men, one of them a British citizen—with sixteen wounded in the police commander’s count, and national mourning begins today, Sunday, November 8, running through Monday, with the city’s mourning through November 11. In the Strait of Hormuz, Saturday evening brought explosions heard on Qeshm Island and at Jask, Sirik, and Bandar Abbas, a report from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy that two oil tankers hit mines on an unauthorized route and caught fire, and an American statement that Central Command late Saturday disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship that ignored warnings and tried to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port. No American statement by midnight claimed the explosions, and no Iranian statement by midnight explained them as a strike. The larger Iran decision promised Thursday was not announced. The count did not move: Mississippi and Alaska stand uncalled for a fourth day, Colorado’s 4th stands uncalled with it, and the talks in Abu Dhabi open Tuesday, November 10, with both delegations now named. Sunday is Diwali’s main day in India, and Poland’s mourning. The desk files the day in that order.

Kraków at Midnight: Three More Bodies, at the Suspect’s Home

The evening’s new fact in Kraków was found 120 miles from the square. CNN’s updated file, filed below, reports that police discovered the bodies of three people—two women and a man—during a search of the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 120 miles north of Kraków, and found many weapons and ammunition in his vehicle. Prime Minister Donald Tusk told the late Saturday crisis meeting in Kraków that there were “strong indications” the three are members of the suspect’s immediate family. That indication is filed as an indication; no identification of the three has been published, and no cause or time of their deaths has been stated by any authority in the files taken in by midnight. The square attack itself stands as the evening filed it: reports began at about 3 p.m. local time, the suspect drove into the Main Market Square firing at random, six people were killed, and police shot and arrested him. The wounded figures and the suspect’s age do not agree across the late files, and the desk prints the disagreement in the cocked hat below.

What Saturday night added on the record is care for the wounded and a country entering mourning. The same CNN file reports the suspect underwent multiple surgeries and is in stable but very critical condition; that the two wounded police officers both underwent surgery and are in stable condition, one shot once and the other three times; that the justice minister said one officer has a non-functioning lung and urgently requires AB+ blood; and that the injured include five foreign nationals, from Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia, and Britain, in an Interior Ministry spokesperson’s account. The British account records the police commander’s statement that three Polish persons, one citizen of Great Britain, and two persons not yet identified make up the six dead, and the foreign secretary’s statement mourning the British national and the other victims. The interior minister’s reading stands where the evening left it: everything points to the shooter having been influenced by far-right ideology, a matter to be investigated. No charge had been announced by midnight, and no motive has been established. Poland’s president will declare national mourning for November 8 and 9; Kraków’s mayor has declared mourning in the city until November 11. Sunday therefore opens in Poland as a day of mourning over nine dead in one case—six in a public square, three in a private house—with the connection between the two sets of deaths stated by the prime minister as a strong indication and by no investigator yet as a finding.

Asunción at Midnight: The Judge Rules, Both Men Held

The question the Evening Watch left at the courthouse door was answered Saturday night. Reuters’ late Asunción file, filed below, reports that Judge Humberto Otazú ordered former President Santiago Peña held in pretrial detention at a military facility, saying detention was necessary to ensure he remained in the country while the case proceeded, and ordered former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo to pretrial detention in a holding center. The charges stand as filed at evening: breach of trust and administration for personal gain against Mr. Peña, and those charges plus producing false public documents against Mr. Carvallo. Prosecutors allege Mr. Peña used his position to influence agencies and state entities to keep large amounts of public money deposited at Ueno despite his financial ties to the lender; he was a shareholder in Ueno’s holding company until March 2025. His attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists Mr. Peña is pleading not guilty and said, “We will submit to the investigation and I am sure that when this investigation is over the result will be the dismissal.” Mr. Peña has denied wrongdoing and said the bank’s problems were a regulatory matter. Mr. Carvallo did not respond to a request for comment in the Reuters file. The two charges against Mr. Peña could carry up to ten years in prison each, the prosecutor said.

The rest of the Asunción file stands settled where the day left it, and the desk keeps the two ledgers separate. The central bank’s Saturday figure stands: the equivalent of $160 million paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers under the deposit guarantee scheme, against a lender that served about three million customers. President Pedro Alliana, sworn in Friday to complete Mr. Peña’s term through August 2028, governs; protests over the Ueno case continue in the accounts filed below, with some sectors calling for early elections. What changed at midnight is narrow and complete: detention, asked at midday and charged at evening, is now ordered. The allegations remain allegations, the plea is not guilty, and the case proceeds with both men in custody—the first former president in this file to pass from removal to a cell in two days, on the record as filed.

Hormuz at Midnight: Explosions on the Coast, Tankers on Fire, a Vessel Disabled

Saturday evening produced three separate reports from one waterway, and the desk files them as three reports, not one event. First, the explosions. Reuters’ Cairo file reports explosions heard Saturday evening in several areas in southern Iran, including on Qeshm Island; that state television suggested the explosions might be linked to Iranian military activities in the waterway; that officials have not confirmed any missile strikes; and that Tasnim, citing a source, said the explosions on Qeshm were not related to missile strikes—while Tasnim also said earlier Saturday that two missiles struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on damage. A second account widens the list of places to Qeshm, Jask, Sirik, and Bandar Abbas, and carries a report of casualties at Jask with no number given, a claim that stands unconfirmed in every other file. Second, the tankers. The Revolutionary Guards Navy said early Sunday, in the Reuters file, that two oil tankers were on fire after hitting mines as they attempted to pass through an “unauthorized route” in the strait; the Iranian military’s late Saturday account, in the Associated Press file filed below, says two tankers hit mines and caught fire and does not identify their flags or destinations. One tanker or two, and at which exit of the strait, are stated differently across the day’s Iranian statements collected in the files below; the desk prints both tellings in the cocked hat. Third, the vessel. Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after it ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port, in the Associated Press file—a confirmed American act, stated by the command itself, in the Gulf of Oman. The same file notes the disclosure follows at least two instances in which the command did not announce strikes it had taken in the region. No file taken in by midnight connects the explosions, the mines, and the disabled ship into one operation, and the desk does not connect them.

The day’s other Iran facts are announcements, and they point in opposite directions, as announcements can. In Tehran, the Revolutionary Guards’ spokesman said the self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometres on ballistic missile ranges “has been lifted for us,” following the supreme leader’s order that threats be answered without geographical limits, in the wire account and the fuller account filed below; both carry the spokesman’s own caution that capability must be demonstrated in practice, and no file shows a missile demonstrated beyond the old limit. In Tampa, Central Command announced Task Force Iron Gate, about twenty military and civilian personnel directed by Admiral Brad Cooper to coordinate with other agencies against the movement of advanced weapons, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea, in the account filed below; the command said its naval blockade has prevented more than $25 billion in Iranian crude exports, a figure that is the command’s own estimate. In Ankara, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told President Trump by telephone that tensions between the United States and Iran should be resolved through diplomacy and that Ankara would continue its peace efforts, and that contacts with Kyiv and Moscow should be intensified, in the readout account filed below; the Turkish readout announced no agreement and no new mediation role. The president’s Friday words stand as the latest American position on the talks—progress claimed, no details given—beside Qatar’s statement that significant progress has been made. The larger decision on resuming the war in full was not announced on Saturday. At midnight the Hormuz file therefore reads: a range limit lifted in words, a task force stood up on paper, a ship disabled at sea, tankers reported burning, explosions unexplained, and diplomacy urged by telephone. Only two of those six items are acts at sea, and both are stated by the side that performed or reported them, without independent confirmation in the files.

Kyiv and Abu Dhabi at Midnight: The Delegations Named, the Damage Counted Three Ways

The talks acquired their full cast on Saturday, and the war acquired a fresh damage ledger the same day. The trilateral talks open in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, November 10 and 11, the first since February. Russia’s delegation will be led by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky and will include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov, and General Staff officer Yuri Zhigarlovsky, in the Reuters account filed below. Ukraine’s team will be led by Rustem Umerov, with Presidential Office chief Kyrylo Budanov also participating, and the United States is expected to be represented by Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, in the second account filed below. The strikes of the night between Friday and Saturday stand as the evening filed them, with the figures unreconciled: President Zelenskyy’s account gives 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones over Kyiv and twelve other regions, four missiles intercepted, and nine people wounded including a child; the wire’s account gives at least five injured in Kyiv; a city account gives two. Russia’s defence ministry confirmed it targeted the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro, saying it facilitated the transport of weaponry and military equipment. In Kyiv, Mr. Zelenskyy’s Saturday address also carried the corruption file forward: he called the alleged crimes in Operation Carthage “frankly shameful, absolutely unacceptable,” said dismissals at the security service have occurred and more personnel decisions will follow, and proposed legislation requiring all security-service employees to publicly declare their assets, in the accounts filed with the Evening Watch. No agreement, draft, or agenda for Abu Dhabi has been published by any side. Tuesday carries the talks’ opening beside the American inflation report and the count’s next deadlines, and nothing in Saturday’s file shortens that list.

The Count at Midnight: A Fourth Day Without a Call

Neither Senate race was called on Saturday, and the published figures for the two races did not move. In Mississippi, the Democrat, Scott Colom, leads the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, by some 2,500 votes in the wire’s tally, at about 49.1 percent to 48.8 percent with the independent candidate just over 2 percent, in the Saturday account and the count update filed below. The estimates of what remains run where they ran: roughly 30,000 ballots possibly outstanding in the wire’s Friday estimate, roughly 20,000 in the Republican estimate carried Saturday, about 3,600 mail ballots in the secretary of state’s Wednesday statement, and an unknown number of affidavit ballots. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day arrive through Tuesday, November 10, voters may resolve ballot problems through the same date, and counties certify by November 13. In Alaska, the Democrat, Mary Peltola, leads the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, by 637 first-choice votes, at 48.2 percent to 47.9 percent with roughly three-quarters of the expected vote reported, unchanged since Wednesday; absentee ballots arrive through November 18, when the ranked-choice tabulation is set, no candidate standing above 50 percent. The legal fronts stand as filed: the Justice Department’s suit over the second candidate named Daniel Sullivan dismissed before the voting, with an appeal pledged, and the Peltola campaign’s Friday records suit over rejected absentee ballots. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide. In the House, Colorado’s 3rd stands called for Representative Jeff Hurd, and Colorado’s 4th stands uncalled, the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, ahead of Representative Lauren Boebert by 3,172 votes at 6 p.m. Friday in the district account filed below—a margin outside the automatic-recount line of about 923 votes, with the cure deadline on November 12—while the Boebert campaign says it is investigating what it calls unusual voting patterns and expects a recount. The count speaks next on Tuesday.

The Week, Settled on Paper: Berkshire’s Quarter

The one scheduled report of Saturday arrived in the morning and closed the market week’s accounts. Berkshire Hathaway’s third quarter, in the accounts filed below: operating earnings of $12.705 billion, down 5.8 percent from $13.485 billion a year earlier; net earnings of $22.112 billion, down 28 percent; insurance underwriting profit down 43 percent; share repurchases of $9.6 billion in the quarter, more than double the second quarter’s $4.5 billion and about $14.4 billion for the year; and cash and Treasury bills at a record $377.435 billion at the end of September, up from $365.514 billion at the end of June. The exchanges were closed, and the week stands as filed at midday: the S&P 500 down 2.7 percent, Brent crude at $98.32, down 13.3 percent on the week. Monday’s open waits on the Hormuz file, as Friday’s close waited on it. Sunday carries no scheduled market item. It carries Poland’s national mourning, beginning today, and in India the main day of Diwali, the festival of lights, whose five days run from Dhanteras on November 6 to Bhai Dooj on November 11, with Lakshmi Puja at dusk today, in the festival account filed below. The desk records both observances in one line each, as the log records what the day is, beside what the day did.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On Kraków’s suspect, the police accounts give his age as 24 and the updated international file gives 25; on the wounded, the afternoon’s official count is fifteen, the police commander’s evening count is sixteen taken to hospital, and one later account counts the wounded suspect among the sixteen. On Hormuz’s tankers, the day’s Iranian statements collected in the files speak of one tanker ablaze at the eastern exit in one telling and two tankers on fire after hitting mines in two others; the desk prints the statements as statements, attributed, and notes that no name, flag, or independent confirmation stands in any of them. On Mississippi’s outstanding ballots, Saturday’s estimates run from about 3,600 mail ballots, in the secretary of state’s figure, to roughly 20,000 in the Republican estimate and roughly 30,000 in the wire’s; the lead is some 2,500 votes in every Saturday account. On Kyiv’s injured, the figures remain two, five, and nine, from a city account, the wire, and the president. Against the triangle, the midnight facts that are single-valued are these: three bodies were found at the Kraków suspect’s home, and six people are dead in the square, with mourning beginning today; Peña and Carvallo are ordered held before trial, on charges both files state the same way, and Mr. Peña pleads not guilty through his attorney; Central Command disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship in the Gulf of Oman, by its own statement, and announced a twenty-person task force in Tampa; explosions were heard across Iran’s Hormuz coast and their cause is confirmed by no authority; the missile-range limit is lifted in words, with no missile shown beyond it; both Abu Dhabi delegations are named and the talks open Tuesday; no Senate race was called; and Berkshire’s quarter is on paper at $12.705 billion in operating earnings and $377.435 billion in cash. Saturday settled a detention, a quarter, and a week. It left open a war at sea, a count in two states, a motive in Kraków, and a negotiation in Abu Dhabi. The log turns to Sunday.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-six items.

 SubjectiveAssociated Press, via Military.com — the military says it fired on a commercial vessel in the Gulf of OmanPublished November 7 at 9:20 p.m. EST: Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after it ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port; the disclosure follows at least two instances in which the command did not announce strikes it had taken in the region; state media also reported explosions on Qeshm Island and several explosions in the port of Jask on Saturday evening, the cause not immediately clear; the Iranian military said late Saturday that two tankers had hit mines in the Hormuz area and caught fire, without identifying their flags or destinations; and the president said Friday the military had carried out new limited strikes against an Iranian air defense system, which he described as minor.

 SubjectiveIsrael.com — blasts across Iran’s Hormuz coast, casualties reported at Jask, the American role unconfirmedNovember 7, updated 11:08 p.m. Israel time: state television widened the list of places where blasts were heard to Qeshm, Jask, Sirik, and Bandar Abbas, all close to the Strait of Hormuz; a correspondent reported people in Iran speaking of casualties resulting from strikes on the port of Jask, without a number, and a senior Iranian official threatening retaliation at the same time; the wire account describes the cause as unclear while the other refers to strikes at Jask; neither report includes a statement from the American military or government about Jask or Qeshm; and the claim of an American strike on an anti-ship missile launcher rests on unofficial channels as relayed by outlets.

 SubjectiveVirginia Times Now — Iran missile range restriction lifted, the Guards sayTehran: the Revolutionary Guards said Saturday the restriction on the range of the country’s missiles has been lifted, spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi saying Iran would demonstrate its ability to respond to threats on the battlefield; the announcement was made at a press conference marking Aerospace Week; the earlier policy was a deliberate limit of 2,000 kilometres; the remarks followed the supreme leader’s warning that threats should receive an immediate response without geographical limits and an order to update target lists covering American and Israeli assets; the spokesman cautioned the statement was not itself proof of a new capability; and the coverage contained no evidence Iran has tested or fielded a missile beyond the former limit.

 SubjectiveSignal Post News — Iran lifts its missile range limit, and says it will prove the new reach in practiceTehran, November 7: the Guards confirmed the self-imposed 2,000-kilometre ceiling on ballistic missile ranges is ended, retiring a nine-year-old reassurance; the spokesman answered that the restriction “has been lifted for us” and added that the new reach has to be demonstrated in practice, not merely announced; the remarks followed the supreme leader’s order of a response to any threat without geographical limits and a review of target lists covering American and Israeli assets; there is no evidence Iran possesses or has demonstrated an operational missile exceeding the former limit, its longest declared systems led by the Khorramshahr-4; and the announcement came a day after American strikes on an Iranian air-defence system amid stalled diplomacy.

 SubjectiveJamaica Inquirer — the United States launches a task force to disrupt Iran’s land-based supply routesCentral Command announced on Saturday it had established a task force to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials, expanding its naval blockade of Iranian ports; Task Force Iron Gate will reinforce the blockade’s success, Admiral Brad Cooper said; based in Tampa, Florida, the task force will coordinate with other agencies on preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea; and a former deputy assistant defence secretary described its role as finding where weapons systems are coming in, how they could be cut off, and how Iran is transporting its energy.

 SubjectiveJBiz News — Erdoğan says he called Trump, reaffirmed Turkish support for American-Iranian diplomacyTurkish President Tayyip Erdoğan told President Trump by phone that Ankara would continue its peace efforts and that tensions between Iran and the United States should be resolved through diplomacy, Erdoğan’s office said on Saturday; Erdoğan also told Trump Turkey would continue to contribute to efforts to end the war in Ukraine and that contacts with both Kyiv and Moscow should be intensified, according to the readout from his office; and the item is filed as a developing story, with no agreement announced in it.

 SubjectiveBosphorus News — Eastern Mediterranean strategic brief, November 7Erdoğan and Trump spoke by telephone on November 7; Erdoğan urged a diplomatic settlement of the American-Iranian confrontation and said Ankara was prepared to support peace efforts, and the call also covered bilateral relations, the Russia-Ukraine war, and contacts with Kyiv and Moscow; the Turkish readout did not identify the American strike near Qeshm Island as a separate agenda item or announce a new mediation role for Türkiye; the Guards’ spokesman said Iran had lifted its missile-range restriction, naming no new ceiling and supplying no test results or deployment details; Qatar’s media office rejected reports that its prime minister had declared the negotiations a failure, saying the two sides were still seeking an agreement; and no date or accepted terms for talks had been announced by the cutoff.

 SubjectiveNation Path India — Russia strikes Kyiv ahead of American-mediated Abu Dhabi peace talksRussia launched ballistic missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and surrounding regions on November 7, damaging residential buildings, energy facilities, and a major bridge, days before negotiations in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 involving Russia, Ukraine, and the United States; Kyiv’s mayor said missile debris struck a five-storey apartment building and another residential building was damaged; Russia’s delegation will be led by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky; Ukraine’s team will be led by Rustem Umerov, with Presidential Office chief Kyrylo Budanov also participating; the United States is expected to be represented by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner; and no comprehensive peace agreement has been reached.

 SubjectiveDevDiscourse, carrying Reuters — Russia pounds power facilities around Kyiv, damages a major bridgeRussian forces hammered energy infrastructure around Kyiv with missiles and drones overnight, straining power supply and heating as temperatures headed towards zero, officials said Saturday, three days before Russia and Ukraine take part in American-brokered talks; explosions rocked Kyiv as waves of ballistic missiles hit and damaged the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River, the mayor said; Russia’s delegation for the first trilateral talks since February will include senior military officials and diplomats including Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov, the Kremlin spokesman told Interfax; the delegation, headed by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, will also include Yuri Zhigarlovsky, Mikhail Galuzin, and military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.

 SubjectiveEuropeSays — Russia strikes Kyiv’s energy infrastructure and the Northern Bridge ahead of the Abu Dhabi talksKyiv faced widespread damage on November 7 after Russia launched 172 attack drones and 36 ballistic missiles at the capital and other regions, striking energy infrastructure, residential housing, and a major bridge over the Dnipro; Russia’s defence ministry confirmed the strike, claiming the bridge was used to transport weapons and military equipment; Ukraine’s president said Russia had launched the 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in a Telegram post with photographs of the damage; Russia’s defence ministry also claimed its air defences shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight, a figure not independently verified; Russia’s delegation will include Medinsky, Ryabkov, Galuzin, Kostyukov, and Zhigarlovsky; and Ukraine’s delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov and include Budanov, Arakhamia, Lytvyn, and Kyslytsia.

 SubjectiveUSA Today — Mississippi and Alaska Senate races still undecided as legal fights loomNearly every major race of the midterms has been called, but not Mississippi and Alaska, where the ballots that will decide two Senate seats are still being sorted, scrutinized, and increasingly litigated; neither will change who controls the chamber, Democrats having claimed the Senate on election night with 54 seats to Republicans’ 44 in the called races; in Mississippi, Scott Colom leads Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by some 2,500 votes according to the Associated Press, which has not called the race, with thousands of affidavit ballots in play and Republicans estimating roughly 20,000 ballots outstanding and voters able to resolve problems through November 10; in Alaska, Mary Peltola leads Senator Dan Sullivan by 637 votes with roughly three-quarters of ballots counted, the Justice Department’s suit was dismissed before the voting, the Peltola campaign opened its own legal front on November 6, and absentee ballots can arrive through November 18, the day of the ranked-choice tabulation.

 SubjectiveElection Central — Alaska and Mississippi Senate race update: they are still counting votesFour days after Election Day, two Senate races remain unresolved and both are remarkably close, and neither can change which party runs the chamber, Democrats having secured at least 54 seats; in Mississippi, Scott Colom holds a lead of roughly 2,500 votes, at about 49.1 percent to 48.8 percent, with all Election Day precincts reported but thousands of absentee and affidavit ballots still being processed, the wire estimating Friday afternoon that roughly 30,000 ballots could still be outstanding, mail ballots arriving through November 10, and counties certifying by November 13; in Alaska, Mary Peltola leads Dan Sullivan by only 637 votes, at 48.2 percent to 47.9 percent, with roughly 74 percent of the expected vote reported, the remaining vote including absentee, remote, and overseas ballots, and a ranked-choice tabulation targeted for November 18 if no candidate reaches a majority.

 SubjectiveAl Jazeera — what is delaying the Senate election results in Mississippi and AlaskaAn explainer of the two undecided races: in Mississippi, mail and affidavit ballots are still being processed under a ten-day window, counties certify by November 13, and the secretary of state counted roughly 3,600 mail ballots outstanding in his Wednesday statement beside an unknown number of affidavit ballots; in Alaska, ranked-choice tabulation is not published until November 18, fifteen days after the election, and nearly a quarter of the vote remains uncounted; as it stands, the Democrats will usher in the 120th Congress on January 3 with a majority of at least 54 seats.

 SubjectiveFocal News — the Boebert campaign cries foul as Laubacher’s lead narrows in Colorado’s 4thRepresentative Lauren Boebert trails the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, by 3,172 votes as of 6 p.m. Friday, a margin of 0.83 percentage points, with more than 97 percent of the vote counted and the race still too close to call; her campaign lawyer said the campaign is investigating unusual voting patterns and expects a recount, though Colorado law requires an automatic recount only at a margin of 0.5 percent or less of the leading candidate’s total—about 923 votes at Friday’s figures, less than one-third of the current gap; a campaign fundraising email misstated the recount law; Ms. Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, led by more than 7,000 votes earlier in the count; and her campaign has not responded publicly to the allegations.

 SubjectiveFadd — Berkshire Hathaway nearly doubles buybacks to $9.6 billion as earnings fallBerkshire Hathaway released its third-quarter results on Saturday, November 7: it spent about $9.6 billion buying its own shares, more than twice the second quarter’s $4.5 billion, bringing 2026 repurchases to about $14.4 billion, and bought roughly another $2 billion in the first four weeks of the fourth quarter; operating earnings came to $12.705 billion, down 5.8 percent from $13.485 billion a year earlier; overall earnings fell 28 percent to $22.112 billion; insurance underwriting profit fell 43 percent to $1.352 billion and insurance investment income fell 14 percent; and cash and equivalents rose 3 percent to $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion at the end of the second quarter.

 SubjectiveShanti — Diwali, the Indian festival of lights and its traditionsDiwali, from the Sanskrit for row of lights, is the biggest festival of the Hindu calendar; its date follows the lunar calendar and falls on the new moon of the month of Kartik, the darkest night of the year; in 2026 the main day falls on Sunday, November 8, and the festival lasts five days, from Friday, November 6 to Tuesday, November 10 in that account’s span; the high point is Lakshmi Puja after dark on the main day, honouring Lakshmi and Ganesha, with dozens of lamps lit, incense, sweets shared, and gifts exchanged; and the account offers the festival to a European reader as a November evening of light against the early dark.

### Six Dead in Kraków, Charges in Asunción, and Kyiv Struck Three Days Before the Talks

Filed as: Edition No. 16 — The Evening Watch · 2026-11-07T18:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-07-evening-watch.html

The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Six Dead in Kraków, Charges in Asunción, and Kyiv Struck Three Days Before the Talks

 The day’s developments whole at 1800: a gunman fired from a car into Kraków’s Main Market Square and killed six people before police shot and arrested him; prosecutors in Asunción charged the removed president and the former central bank chief and asked a court to jail both pending trial, while $160 million went out to nearly 1.2 million savers; Iran’s Guards lifted the self-imposed limit on missile ranges while Washington and Doha both said the talks had made progress; Russian missiles struck Kyiv three days before the Abu Dhabi talks, and Moscow named its delegation; the first considered responses to the Miller appointment set the terms of the next two years in Washington; and no Senate race was called for a fourth day.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Saturday, November 7, 2026. This edition completes the day continued in Edition No. 14, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400, and Edition No. 15, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the evening figures differ from the midday figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Evening in Brief

Saturday produced one atrocity, one indictment, and three statements of position, and closed nothing the week left open. In Kraków, at about 3 p.m. local time, a man drove into the Main Market Square and fired at random from his car, killing six people—four women and two men—and wounding at least fifteen, two of them police officers, before officers shot and arrested him three minutes after the first report, in the interior minister’s account; the minister said in his evening briefing that everything points to the shooter having been influenced by far-right ideology, a matter he said will be investigated, and the president will declare national mourning for November 8 and 9. In Asunción, prosecutors charged former President Santiago Peña with breach of trust and administration for personal gain and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo with those charges and producing false public documents, asked a court to hold both men in pretrial detention and freeze their assets, and the central bank reported $160 million paid out to nearly 1.2 million Ueno savers under the deposit guarantee. In Tehran, the Revolutionary Guards’ spokesman said the self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometres on ballistic missile ranges “has been lifted for us,” following the supreme leader’s order that threats be answered without geographical limits; no file on the shelf shows an Iranian missile demonstrated beyond the old limit. In Washington, the responses to Friday’s appointment of Stephen Miller as chief of staff, effective Monday, divided on the record: allies called the pick perfect and critics, including one Republican congressman, called it a misreading of the voters’ verdict, while in Houston the mayor’s order limiting police cooperation with federal immigration officers took effect as the week’s first local answer to the election. On Iran, the president’s Friday words stand as the latest American position—“We’ve made a lot of progress with Iran”—beside Qatar’s statement that significant progress has been made; no agreement, no text, and no larger strike decision had been announced by 1800. Kyiv was struck by Russian missiles in the night, three days before the Abu Dhabi talks open, and Moscow named its delegation on Saturday. The count did not move: Mississippi and Alaska stand uncalled for a fourth day, and the markets, closed Saturday, stand where Friday left them. The desk files the day in that order.

Kraków: Six Dead in the Main Market Square

The attack began at about 3 p.m. local time and the suspect was in custody minutes later. Reuters’ Kraków file, filed below, reports that police began receiving calls at about 3 p.m. that an assailant had opened fire from a car at people in the Main Market Square, the historic centre of Poland’s second-largest city; that the dead are four women and two men; that the alleged gunman is a 24-year-old Polish citizen who wore military-style clothes and used military weapons, with many weapons and ammunition found in his vehicle; and that police shot and arrested him. A police spokesperson told a broadcaster the weapon was an AR-15 rifle and that the man held a firearms licence. The account of the official statements records that the toll was first given as five dead and was later confirmed at six dead and fifteen injured by the regional government office; that two police officers are among the injured, one of them shot three times and in very critical condition, with surgery under way; and that police denied reports that an officer had died or that a second perpetrator was being sought—“The only known perpetrator of the incident is in police custody.” The suspect has not been named publicly by the police. The defence minister denied reports that he was a member of the armed forces, in the accounts filed below.

The evening added the government’s first reading of the motive, and it is filed as a reading, not a finding. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński, in his evening briefing as carried in the Reuters file, said: “Everything points to the fact that the shooter was influenced by far-right ideology, a matter that will also be subject to investigation.” He said five foreigners were among the sixteen wounded taken to hospital—one more than the fifteen in the afternoon’s official count—and that four of the dead had been identified, one of them a foreigner; Portugal’s foreign ministry said a Portuguese woman was among the injured. A later account filed below reports the national police chief saying a British citizen is among the dead, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk, speaking in Kraków after meeting the security services, calling the attack terrorism and saying Poland has not had such a drastic case before. Mr. Tusk’s afternoon statement asked politicians of all stripes not to exploit the tragedy and said all the circumstances will be established. President Karol Nawrocki’s spokesperson said he will declare national mourning on November 8 and 9; the city has declared mourning through November 11. Condolences arrived from President Zelenskyy of Ukraine and from the European Union’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, in the same file. No charge against the suspect had been announced by 1800 ET, and no motive has been established by any court or investigator on the record.

Asunción at Evening: Charges Filed, Detention Asked, Savers Paid

The case the midday edition left at the prosecutor’s door was filed in the afternoon. Reuters’ Asunción file, updated after the appearance, reports that prosecutors on Saturday charged former President Santiago Peña with breach of trust and administration for personal gain and asked a court to jail him pending trial; that former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo was charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents, and administration for personal gain, with his pretrial detention also sought; that prosecutors allege Peña used his position to influence agencies and state entities to keep large amounts of public money deposited at Ueno despite his financial ties to the lender; and that the two charges against Peña could carry up to ten years in prison each, in the prosecutor’s statement. A second account adds that both men declined to say anything at the hearing, that prosecutors asked for both men’s assets to be frozen and for six months to formulate the final case, that twenty-seven people have been charged in total, and that a judge has ordered six former Ueno directors held in pretrial detention. Peña’s lawyer, Ricardo Preda, rejected pretrial detention before the charges were filed, saying nothing justified it. Peña has denied wrongdoing and said the bank’s problems were a regulatory matter. The charges are charges; the detention request is a request; a judge has not ruled on it, and no court has ruled on any allegation in the case.

The other half of the day in Asunción is money moving back to savers, and a new government forming under protest. The central bank said on Saturday that the equivalent of $160 million had been paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers under the deposit guarantee scheme, in the Reuters file—the first payment figure of the crisis, against a bank that served about three million customers and held as much as $850 million in public money. The fuller account of the week filed below records that President Pedro Alliana’s first decree appointed Ariel Martínez as minister of the interior, a post he held in 2018, with Juan Carlos Baruja arriving at Public Works; that the prosecutorial hypothesis examines deposits by public bodies and social security entities between 2023 and 2026 and allegedly irregular credits to companies linked to Grupo Vázquez; and that protests over the Ueno case continue, with protesters and opposition sectors questioning Alliana and some calling for early elections. The guarantee’s structure stands as the central bank published it: a first group paid in full up to ten million guaraníes, an advance of up to forty minimum wages, and a coverage limit of seventy-five minimum wages per depositor—three different figures, not three payments to be added. What Alliana promised in words, that those affected will recover their funds, and what the guarantee pays in stages, remain two different statements, and the desk keeps them separate.

Washington at Evening: The Miller Appointment Read From Every Side

Friday’s appointment produced its considered readings on Saturday, and they divide cleanly. The facts stand as filed Friday: Susie Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday evening; the president announced Stephen Miller, his deputy chief of staff and the architect of the administration’s immigration enforcement programme, as her successor, effective Monday; Mrs. Wiles will move to the president’s political operation; and the president told CBS News he intends further changes, saying of his Cabinet, “I love my Cabinet. I think they’re good. But I’ll be doing maybe a few changes.” Saturday’s analysis, filed below, reads the appointment as the president doubling down after first suggesting openness to working with Democrats: allies who urged the change argued Mr. Miller had proven he could carry out the president’s programme without a learning period and could repair the party’s standing with its own movement; Steve Bannon called him “a perfect pick.” The other reading is on the same record: Representative Marlin Stutzman of Indiana, a Republican, said in a local radio appearance, “We lost Latinos because of the deportation look,” singling out Mr. Miller, and added that the party must wake up to being in the minority. Representative Robert Garcia, the incoming Oversight leadership’s ranking member, said, “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.” Representative Chellie Pingree of Maine called the choice a move “from very bad to worse than you could possibly imagine.” An immigration-reform advocate quoted in the analysis said calls to work with the president on reform are not realistic while Mr. Miller is in the White House. The president’s own words on the pick were: “Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it. Very good politically. And he’s a very good man.” Mr. Miller posted that serving as chief of staff is “the privilege of my lifetime” and that “the mission now is more clear than ever.” Both readings agree on one fact: the appointment takes effect Monday, and the two years of divided government begin with it.

The election’s first local consequence in Texas took effect the same weekend. Reuters’ Houston file reports that Mayor John Whitmire on Friday ordered the city’s police to curtail cooperation with federal immigration officers: officers on routine stops are barred from alerting Immigration and Customs Enforcement solely on the basis of a civil immigration warrant, and may notify the agency only when the person is also being arrested on a jailable offence. The mayor said he acted after consulting the state’s newly elected governor, lieutenant governor, and comptroller, to “reduce fear and anxiety” across the city and because “elections matter.” Police Chief J. Noe Diaz said he supported the change and the department had begun implementing it. The order reverses a policy the mayor adopted in April under pressure from Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid on Tuesday; department figures carried in the accounts filed below show officers contacted the agency nearly 200 times from April through September and handed people directly to it at least 36 times. The order does not bar federal agents from operating in Houston on their own authority. It is the first such order of the post-election week on the shelf, and it was made by a mayor of the president’s opponents’ party in the largest city of a state his party swept on Tuesday—filed as the local record, under the same roof as the appointment above it, because the evening file is the day whole.

Iran at Evening: The Range Limit Lifted, Progress Claimed on Both Sides, No Decision Announced

Tehran’s announcement of the day is a policy ending, stated by the Guards in one sentence. Tasnim’s file reports that Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, announced at a press conference for the force’s Aerospace Week that restrictions on the range of Iran’s missiles have been lifted, saying the country must demonstrate its expanded capabilities in practice rather than merely make statements. The fuller account adds that the remarks followed Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei’s order of an immediate and effective response to any threat without geographical limits, and a review of the military’s target database to include American and Israeli assets. The wire’s account puts the change plainly: the self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometres, in place since 2017 under the former supreme leader, is ended, suggesting Iran may seek weapons able to reach more distant targets. Every account on the shelf carries the same caution, and the desk repeats it as part of the fact: no file shows Iran possessing or demonstrating an operational missile beyond the old limit, and General Mohebbi himself said the capability must be shown in practice before it is claimed. A restraint is lifted; a weapon is not thereby in hand.

Against that announcement, the diplomatic file gained words from both principals and no paper. The president, speaking to reporters in West Palm Beach on Friday in the account filed below, confirmed the limited strikes on Iranian air defences near Qeshm Island—“We do minor strikes”; “we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five”—and said repeatedly that his administration is speaking with Tehran’s representatives: “We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal. We’ve made a lot of progress with Iran.” He gave no details of the progress. Qatar’s prime minister said the same day, in the midday file, that significant progress had been made and the aim is a good agreement rather than a perfect one, and Qatar’s media office denied reports that the talks had failed. The Qatari proposal, as reported in the accounts filed below, would have Washington lift its blockade and release some frozen Iranian funds, Iran admit international inspectors to damaged sites, and the Strait of Hormuz reopen on the arrangement’s second day, without Iran surrendering its nuclear stockpiles; Tehran’s deputy security chief said Iran is not satisfied with paper commitments and must see practical steps, and Tehran’s own seven conditions stand unmet and unwithdrawn. The explosions reported from Qeshm in the night remain unconfirmed as to origin and damage, and the United States has not announced any new attack. The larger decision promised on Thursday—whether to resume the war in full—had not been announced at 1800 on Saturday. Progress is claimed in Washington and in Doha; it is described in neither capital; and the missile announcement in Tehran is the day’s only new fact with a text behind it.

Kyiv and Abu Dhabi: Missiles in the Night, a Delegation Named, Three Days Out

Kyiv was struck in the night between Friday and Saturday, and the counts of the injured do not agree. The Associated Press file reports missile explosions in Kyiv early Saturday leaving at least five people injured, damaging homes and commercial properties, closing traffic on a bridge over the Dnipro River, and triggering new power and water outages. A second account puts the injured at two and records Mayor Vitali Klitschko reporting explosions in the suburbs as missiles targeted infrastructure, after President Zelenskyy’s Friday warning that Russia was preparing strikes on energy facilities, bridges, and civilian infrastructure. Mr. Zelenskyy’s Saturday statement, in the accounts filed below, gives the barrage at 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones over Kyiv and twelve other regions, four missiles intercepted, and nine people wounded including a child; Russia’s defence ministry confirmed it targeted the Northern Bridge, saying it facilitated the transport of weaponry and military equipment. The desk prints the three injury figures as three figures—two, five, and nine—from three hours and three sources, and does not choose among them. No deaths in Kyiv had been confirmed in the accounts taken in by 1800.

The talks the missiles precede acquired their cast on Saturday. The Kremlin spokesman told Interfax, in the Saturday accounts filed below, that Russia’s delegation to Abu Dhabi will be led by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky and will include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov, and a General Staff officer, Yuri Zhigarlovsky. The American president’s Thursday position stands: after meeting the Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev privately, he predicted a big agreement involving more than Ukraine, possibly all of Europe, and gave no details and said he had not met the Ukrainian delegation. Ukraine’s president, in the interview account filed below, said he does not know many details of the framework being floated, warned that a deal between Russia and Europe would not be simple and could be dangerous, and held that ending the war comes first and guarantees second—the same position as his Thursday demand that guarantees be clear on paper. The talks open Tuesday, November 10, the first trilateral meeting since February. In his Saturday evening address, Mr. Zelenskyy also spoke to a second file: the corruption investigation, Operation Carthage, in which anti-corruption authorities have charged senior security and law-enforcement officials with shielding a criminal ring. Reuters’ Kyiv file reports him calling the alleged crimes “frankly shameful, absolutely unacceptable,” saying dismissals at the security service have already occurred and more personnel decisions will follow, and proposing legislation requiring all security-service employees to publicly declare their assets. A court on Friday ordered a former general of the service arrested pending bail. The allegations are allegations; the dismissals and the bill are acts.

The Count at Evening: A Fourth Day Without a Call

Neither Senate race was called on Saturday, and the day’s contribution to the file is an explanation of the wait. The explainer filed below sets out the machinery: in Mississippi, mail and affidavit ballots are still being processed under a ten-day window, counties certify by November 13, and the secretary of state counted roughly 3,600 mail ballots outstanding in his Wednesday statement beside an unknown number of affidavit ballots; in Alaska, ranked-choice tabulation is not published until November 18, fifteen days after the election, and nearly a quarter of the vote remains uncounted. The Saturday account of the two races carries the standing figures: Scott Colom ahead of Cindy Hyde-Smith by some 2,500 votes in Mississippi in the wire’s tally, with Republicans estimating roughly 20,000 ballots outstanding—an estimate ten thousand below the figure in circulation at midday—and voters able to resolve ballot problems through November 10; and Mary Peltola ahead of Dan Sullivan by 637 votes in Alaska, with the legal fronts in that race opened by both sides, the Justice Department’s suit before the voting and the Peltola campaign’s records suit on Friday. Democrats will hold at least 54 Senate seats in the 120th Congress whatever the two races decide; what remains open is the size of the majority, for a fourth day. Colorado’s 4th District stands where Friday left it, Eileen Laubacher ahead of Lauren Boebert by 3,278 votes, uncalled. Tuesday, November 10 now carries the next Alaska update, Mississippi’s ballot deadline, both congressional parties’ leadership elections, consumer prices, and the opening of the Abu Dhabi talks.

Europe’s Hoaxes and the Week’s Settled Markets

Friday’s third wave of hoax bomb threats is the evening’s European file, and its totals also disagree. The fullest account, filed below, counts at least 18 flights disrupted on Friday to or from nine countries, while the European transport commissioner put Friday’s total at 11; nine of the flights used Prague’s airport, Hungary scrambled fighter jets to escort three threatened aircraft, and four aircraft over France landed at Paris Orly for inspection. Every threatened aircraft landed safely and no explosives were found on any plane or at any site. The threats spread on Friday to newsrooms: Ireland’s broadcaster evacuated its Dublin headquarters and ran pre-recorded programming for hours, other Irish outlets emptied their offices, and a British broadcaster confirmed it had received a threat. Friday’s emails were signed with a name claiming leadership of the group behind the week’s hoaxes; a different signature on Thursday’s threats named a movement whose founder denied involvement and said the group has not existed since 2021. Investigators have found no evidence that a hostile state or a terror group is directing the hoaxes. Spain’s foreign minister said the identical methods across so many countries could not be coincidence and called the most reasonable assumption “an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare”; Ireland’s prime minister said the episode showed how relatively simple it can be to disrupt the normal operation of society. Both statements are on the record; the authorship of the threats is not. The markets add nothing to the day: the exchanges are closed, and the week stands settled as filed at midday—the S&P 500 down 2.7 percent, Brent crude at $98.32, down 13.3 percent, and Berkshire Hathaway’s third quarter, operating earnings down 5.8 percent and cash at a record $377.4 billion, as the day’s one scheduled report. Monday’s open waits on the Iran file, as it waited on Friday.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On Kraków’s wounded, the afternoon’s official count is fifteen and the interior minister’s evening figure is sixteen taken to hospital; the desk prints both and notes the hour of each. On Kyiv’s injured, the figures are two, five, and nine, from a city account, the wire, and the president, and no confirmed death stands in any of them. On the hoax flights, the counts are eleven and eighteen for the same Friday. On Mississippi’s outstanding ballots, the estimates in circulation on Saturday run from roughly 20,000 to roughly 30,000. Against the triangle, the evening’s load-bearing facts are single-valued: six people are dead in Kraków and the only known perpetrator is in police custody; Peña and Carvallo stand charged, detention and an asset freeze are asked and not yet granted, and $160 million has been paid to nearly 1.2 million savers; the missile-range limit has been lifted in words, with no missile shown beyond it; progress on Iran is claimed in Washington and Doha and described in neither; Russia has named its Abu Dhabi delegation and the talks open Tuesday; Stephen Miller takes the chief of staff’s office on Monday; Houston’s order is in effect; no race was called; and the Shenzhen meeting of three presidents, eleven days out, received no new word. Saturday’s file therefore closes as it opened in the brief: one atrocity, answered by an arrest and an investigation; one presidency, answered by a charge sheet and a payment ledger; two wars, answered by announcements and preparations; and an election, answered so far by an appointment, a mayor’s order, and a count that will not move until Tuesday. The log proceeds to midnight.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-seven items.
